medium.conteudo_html:
ally are, once you strip away the hype
A plain-language guide to how LLMs think, learn, and occasionally lie with total confidence
Imagine a chef who has read every cookbook ever published. Every recipe, every food blog, every scribbled note in every margin of every kitchen manual from the last hundred years. This chef can tell you, instantly and eloquently, how to make a soufflé rise, why you should rest a steak, and what wine pairs with duck confit.
There’s just one catch: this chef has never actually cooked anything. Not once. Everything they know comes from reading about food, not tasting it, burning it, or fixing a broken sauce at 8pm with hungry guests at the table.
That, in a nutshell, is a large language model. And once you understand that one idea, almost everything else about LLMs — their brilliance, their blind spots, their strange confidence — starts to make sense.
Read every cookbook → Predicts the next word → Fluent output
Figure 1: The whole trick of an LLM in three steps — no tasting required.
What’s actually in the cookbook
An LLM’s "cookbook" is a staggering pile of text: books, websites, articles, forum posts, code repositories, transcripts, and more — often hundreds of billions of words. During training, the model doesn’t memorize this text like a filing cabinet. Instead, it studies the patterns in how words follow other words, across every context imaginable, and compresses those patterns into billions of numerical values called parameters.
Think of parameters as the chef’s intuition, built entirely from reading. After enough cookbooks, the chef starts to sense that "sear" tends to appear near "high heat," that "braise" goes with "low and slow," that a recipe calling for saffron probably isn’t a budget dish. None of this is explicit knowledge the chef looked up — it’s a feel for the shape of the language, formed by exposure.
The core mechanism: at every step, the model looks at the text so far and asks one question — "given everything I’ve read, what word is most likely to come next?" It answers that question, adds the word, and asks again. Do that a few hundred times and you get a paragraph. �
LLM_Blog_Post.pdf
Tokens: the ingredients of language
Before any of this happens, text gets chopped into small chunks called tokens — sometimes whole words, sometimes fragments like "un," "believ," and "able." The model never sees raw sentences the way you do; it sees a stream of these ingredient-sized pieces, each converted into a long list of numbers.
This is where the cookbook metaphor gets literal. Just as a recipe is really a sequence of ingredients and actions, a sentence, to the model, is a sequence of tokens. Generation is the model reaching into its enormous pantry of possible next-tokens and pulling out the one that statistically fits best, given everything that came before.
Example:
Input sentence:
"The soufflé began to..."
Tokenized:
The souf flé began to ?
Model predicts:
"rise" (74%), "collapse" (15%), "brown" (6%)...
Figure 2: Splitting text into tokens, then predicting what comes next.
Training: tasting menus without a tongue
During training, the model is repeatedly shown a snippet of text with the next word hidden, asked to guess it, and then told the right answer. It adjusts its internal parameters slightly to be less wrong next time. Multiply this by trillions of examples and you get a system that has developed an extraordinarily refined sense of linguistic probability — without ever once understanding what a soufflé is, why it rises, or what it’s like to eat one.
This is the crucial distinction between our chef and a real one. A human chef who burns a dish tastes the failure, smells it, remembers the sting of it. An LLM "corrected" during training never experiences anything — it just nudges some numbers. The chef becomes brilliant at describing cooking without ever developing the embodied, sensory understanding that comes from actually doing it. �
LLM_Blog_Post.pdf
Where the metaphor bites: hallucination
Ask our well-read chef for a recipe that technically doesn’t exist — say, a "Genovese soufflé tart" — and instead of saying "that’s not a real dish," they might confidently invent one. It’ll sound completely plausible: proper ratios, sensible technique, convincing plating advice. It will also be entirely made up.
This is exactly what happens when an LLM "hallucinates." Because the model’s whole job is producing statistically plausible text, not verified fact, it will sometimes generate answers that are fluent, confident, and false.
It isn’t lying in the human sense — it has no concept of truth to violate. It’s doing precisely what it was built to do: continue the pattern in the most likely-sounding way, even when the most likely-sounding way is fiction. �
LLM_Blog_Post.pdf
"A model that has read a million recipes can describe cooking beautifully. It still can’t taste the sauce."
So what is it actually good at?
Despite never cooking, our chef would still be an incredible resource in a kitchen. Ask them to explain a technique, suggest substitutions, summarize the differences between five pastry styles, or translate a French recipe on the fly, and they’d excel. The breadth of exposure is a genuine strength, not a gimmick.
Main strengths
Summarizing and rephrasing — condensing or restructuring text is close to the core skill: predicting likely, coherent language.
Drafting and brainstorming — generating plausible first drafts across an enormous range of styles and topics.
Explaining known concepts — the "cookbook" contains explanations of almost everything, so retrieving and rephrasing them is a natural fit.
Pattern-based coding help — code follows strict, learnable structure, which plays to the model’s strengths.
Where it struggles
LLMs struggle where grounded, verified, real-world truth is required rather than plausible-sounding language:
Precise facts
Current events past its training data
Arithmetic requiring exactness
Genuinely novel reasoning that no cookbook ever described �
LLM_Blog_Post.pdf
Why this metaphor matters more than the jargon
Most explanations of LLMs reach for words like "transformer," "attention mechanism," and "embedding space" — accurate, but not exactly illuminating for a general reader.
What actually matters, if you’re deciding how much to trust an AI’s answer, is this single mental model:
You’re talking to something that has read everything and tasted nothing.
Practical takeaway: treat an LLM like a brilliant, widely-read assistant who has never once verified anything firsthand. Wonderful for a first draft, a summary, or an explanation of something well-documented. Worth double-checking for anything where being wrong actually matters.
Why the chef sounds so sure of themselves
One of the strangest features of LLMs is that their confidence doesn’t track their accuracy.
Our chef doesn’t hedge more when discussing an obscure regional dish they’ve only read about once versus a classic French technique covered in a thousand cookbooks — the tone of certainty is roughly the same either way.
That’s because the model isn’t tracking "how sure am I this is true," it’s tracking "how statistically typical does this sentence sound."
Confident, well-formed language is what gets rewarded during training, regardless of whether the underlying claim happens to be accurate. �
LLM_Blog_Post.pdf
A human expert who’s unsure will usually signal it — a pause, a qualifier, a "I think, but check me on this."
An LLM’s hallucinated answer can come out in exactly the same polished, assured prose as its correct ones. The surface confidence gives you almost no information about reliability, which is precisely why it’s worth treating fluent-sounding claims with a bit of healthy skepticism, especially on anything specific, numeric, or obscure.
The chef, ten years from now
Newer systems are starting to get a spoon, so to speak — tools that let a model search the web, run code, or check a calculator instead of guessing.
That’s less like a smarter chef and more like a well-read chef finally being handed real ingredients and a working kitchen. It helps enormously. It still doesn’t replace the years of scars, instincts, and small sensory judgments that come from actually cooking.
Understanding that gap — between fluent description and lived experience — is probably the single most useful piece of AI literacy anyone can have right now.
It won’t make the technology less impressive. If anything, it makes it easier to see exactly where its genuine talents lie, and exactly where to reach for a second opinion.
The next time an LLM answers a question with total confidence, picture the chef: extraordinarily well-read, genuinely helpful, and still, in the most important sense, someone who has never once been in the kitchen. �

medium.titulo: The Future of Engineering Isn’t AI Alone — It’s the Personal Digital Twin
medium.resumo: The Problem No One Is Talking About
medium.conteudo_html:
The Problem No One Is Talking About

Engineering leaders are right to be excited about AI tooling. The productivity gains for individual developers are real. But there is a problem emerging underneath that productivity, and it is not the one most people are watching for.

Think about how teams operate today. One engineer uses an AI assistant to build a capability. Another engineer, on another team, uses their own AI assistant to build something similar. Neither assistant knows what the other is doing. Neither agent has awareness of the broader engineering context.

The result is predictable: duplicated code, duplicated logic, and duplicated effort.

But the duplication is the symptom, not the disease. The real issue is execution: every agent is making decisions in isolation. No agent sees the whole. We’ve handed more and more of the building over to AI without giving any of it a shared picture of what is already being built.

Individual execution is getting faster while organizational execution pulls apart at the seams.

This is not a tooling problem. It is an orchestration problem. And you cannot orchestrate what cannot see beyond itself.

Introducing the Personal Digital Twin

A typical AI agent knows its task and its local context — the project it is working in, the system it is touching, the prompt in front of it. Its awareness begins and ends at the boundary of that work. Spin up a swarm of them and you get role-specialized agents — coordinator, implementor, verifier — coordinating around a task. That is the dominant pattern in the market today, and it is genuinely useful. But every agent in that swarm is still defined by the job, not by a person.

A Personal Digital Twin is defined by a person. It is paired one-to-one with a specific engineer and mirrors that human — their work patterns, their decisions, the cross-project context they carry in their head, the way they have solved problems before. It does not just know the project in front of it. It knows what its engineer has built across every project, and it stays aware of what other engineers’ Twins are doing across the organization, peer-to-peer.

That difference is not cosmetic. A task-scoped agent forgets the person the moment the task changes. A Twin persists with the person across tasks, teams, and time — which is exactly the context that gets lost when work is fragmented across an org.

What This Unlocks

When AI agents become aware of one another, Reuse becomes the default. The system starts to compound instead of sprawl. Every capability builds on the last instead of growing up beside it — so the codebase gets smaller as it gets more capable, not bigger.

Second, coordination stops being an accident. In most engineering organizations, the bottleneck was never individual output. It was the lack of shared context across teams, systems, and workstreams. Personal Digital Twins surface that context before the divergence happens, not in a postmortem months later.

Third, the human-machine relationship gets sharper. The engineer is not replaced and is not merely sped up. The Twin absorbs the context-tracking and signal-processing no human can hold across an entire org. The engineer keeps the judgment calls.

The Technology Is Ready

It is tempting to frame this as the future of engineering. But I do not think this is a distant future. The real constraints are time, investment, and execution.

Across the industry, people are already beginning to think about how to orchestrate and coordinate AI agents. The opportunity now is to define what that orchestration should look like.

At KMS Technology, this is one of the reasons we created Velox: to bring orchestration, coordination, and context awareness into the way AI agents support software engineering teams.

Because AI agents working alone will only take us so far. AI agents working together — with context — can change how engineering organizations operate.

A Final Thought

The teams that win in the next era of software engineering will not simply be the ones that adopt the most AI tools. They will be the ones that execute as a coordinated whole instead of a collection of fast, disconnected parts.

The Personal Digital Twin is one way to get there: an AI partner for every engineer, aware not only of the individual’s work, but of the broader engineering ecosystem around them.

The technology is here. The question is who moves first.

medium.titulo: Claude Docs, Slides, and Cowork: What’s New and What’s Worth Using
medium.resumo: Docs, Slides, and one Claude — whats useful in the Sep 2026 beta, and what still isnt’
medium.conteudo_html:
Docs, Slides, and one Claude — whats useful in the Sep 2026 beta, and what still isnt’

I’ve been bouncing between chat dumps and Google Docs for months. Draft in Claude, copy-paste into Docs, lose the thread, paste a comment back into chat, wonder which version is current. It’s workable. Also a bit ridiculous for something sold as “knowledge work.”

Last month it ate an evening. Tuesday afternoon I’d been in Claude on a long research brief — three sources, a structure I liked, a few paragraphs I’d asked it to soften. Around nine I dumped the lot into Google Docs so a friend could leave comments overnight. Wednesday lunch: their notes in Docs, my replies half in the Docs thread and half pasted back into the original Claude chat, plus a third tab with an older paste from Tuesday morning. I emailed the wrong one. Not a disaster — just the version without the softener and with a stale intro. Another hour of apologetic tidying. Same bounce that’s been annoying me for months; that time it actually cost something.

Mid-September 2026, Anthropic shipped a direct answer to that mess: **Claude Docs** and **Claude Slides** in beta, plus a quieter but bigger change — Cowork and chat are becoming **one Claude**. No more picking a mode and hoping you guessed right.

I haven’t lived inside the beta for weeks. I’ve read the launch posts, the Help Centre, and the early coverage. What follows is what’s new, what I’d actually use, what I’d skip, and who should care — without the launch-day glitter.

## What’s new

### One Claude (Cowork + chat)

Cowork started as a separate place for longer, multi-step work. Useful, and also a small tax every time you had to decide: is this a chat, or is this a Cowork job?

Anthropic’s fix is blunt. Chat and Cowork merge. Claude decides whether a request needs a quick reply or longer agentic work. Design and Artifacts capabilities are meant to be available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have.

> The useful part isn’t “agentic” as a slogan. It’s not having to route yourself before you can get work done.

Rollout: Pro and Max first on web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks. Team and Free later. Enterprise admins get notice (at least 30 days) before anything changes for their organisations. There’s nothing to turn on for Pro/Max when it lands — and you can still use Claude as ordinary chat.

### Claude Docs

Docs are living rich-text documents inside the conversation: headings, tables, multi-tab notebooks, comments that look like Google Docs. Claude can ask clarifying questions before drafting, leave comments explaining choices, and respond when you `@Claude` in a comment thread.

Practical details that matter:

- Saved in **Artifacts**, so you can find them again from any chat
- Share by link (opening a shared doc requires a Claude account)
- Export to **Word, PDF, Markdown, or Google Docs**
- You can ask Claude to turn a Doc into Slides
- Collaborative editing with people who have edit access

### Claude Slides

Presentations from chat: draft a deck, edit it, present from Claude, or export to **PowerPoint or PDF**. Same conversation context as the Doc you just wrote — which is the bit that reduces the “slides don’t match the report” tax.

Both Docs and Slides sit alongside Claude Design as beta productivity tools on paid plans.

## Availability (the unromantic bit)

Docs and Slides are **beta on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise — not Free**.

- **Pro / Max / Team:** on by default (you can turn Docs off in Settings → Capabilities)
- **Enterprise:** off until an owner enables them (Organisation settings → Artifacts)
- **Not available yet** for orgs on CMEK, zero data retention (ZDR), or HIPAA-ready configurations

Usage counts toward your normal Claude limits. A long doc pulled from several sources costs more than a short reply. That’s expected; just don’t treat Docs like free unlimited Google Docs with a chat sidebar.

## What’s actually worth using vs ignore-for-now

### Worth using

- **One Claude for messy, multi-step work.** If you’ve ever started a report in chat, realised halfway it needed files and connectors, and restarted in Cowork — this is the feature. I did that last fortnight: started a source roundup in ordinary chat, hit the wall when I needed a PDF and a spreadsheet open together, opened Cowork, lost the half-finished framing, spent twenty minutes reconstructing the brief. Let Claude choose the depth; keep your prompts specific about audience and deadline.
- **Docs as the place the draft *lives*.** Status reports, briefs, onboarding guides, meeting one-pagers — anything you’d previously dump into a Google Doc and immediately lose context for. Especially if you’re already on Pro/Max and living in Claude for research and writing.
- **Doc → Slides in the same thread.** When the narrative and the deck need to stay aligned, generating both from one conversation saves a fair bit of grief. I’ve not lived in the Slides beta — but I know the pain it’s aimed at. After that brief mess I built five slides in a separate tool from memory of the chat. Two of them still had the old framing. The Doc→Slides pitch is basically: don’t rely on what you remember at 11pm.
- **`@Claude` in comments.** This is closer to how people actually edit: highlight a paragraph, ask for a fix, keep the discussion attached to the text.

### Skip for now (or treat carefully)

- **Treating Claude Docs as your system of record.** No version history yet. Deleting a doc is permanent — no trash. For anything that needs audit trails or rollback, export early and keep the canonical copy elsewhere.
- **Enterprise compliance workflows that need CMEK / ZDR / HIPAA-ready.** Not supported yet. Don’t plan a migration around a beta that your org literally can’t turn on.
- **Heavy mobile editing.** On iOS/Android you can view docs; starting from templates, editing, and changing sharing settings still wants web or desktop.
- **External sharing on Team/Enterprise.** Docs stay inside the organisation. Fine for internal work; useless if your workflow is “send this link to the client.”
- **charts that “just stay fresh.”** Claude can build charts from connected apps; they don’t auto-refresh. You’ll need to ask for a refresh when the spreadsheet moves.

### Worth using / Skip for now

**Worth using**

- Living drafts that stay attached to the chat that produced them
- Clarifying questions + comment threads with `@Claude`
- Export when you need Word / Google Docs / Markdown / PPTX / PDF
- One Claude when you don’t want to pick a mode

**Skip for now**

- Versioned, regulated, or externally shared document workflows
- Mobile-first editing and sharing
- Assuming charts track live data
- Free-tier hopes (Docs/Slides aren’t on Free)

## Honest limitations

Anthropic is clear enough in the Help Centre that you don’t need spin:

- No version history yet
- No comment-only access (view or edit)
- Charts/diagrams don’t update automatically
- Team/Enterprise can’t share docs outside the org
- CMEK / ZDR / HIPAA-ready orgs: not yet
- Compliance API doesn’t yet log edits/comments inside a doc
- Mobile is view-mostly for editing and sharing controls

I’d also watch usage burn. Agentic Cowork-style work and long multi-source drafts chew tokens. If you’re on Pro and already tight mid-month, treat Docs as a drafting surface, not a place to regenerate the same 20-page brief five times.

## Who should care

**Writers, researchers, PMs, and analysts** who already live in Claude and hate the paste-into-Docs loop — this is for you. Anthropic is competing with Gemini’s grip on Google Workspace by pulling more of the document lifecycle *into* the chat. Google still wins on suite habit and external collaboration; Claude is betting you’ll stay if the draft never leaves the conversation.

**Team leads** should care about the org boundaries: internal collaboration yes, client-facing link share no (on Team/Enterprise). **Enterprise buyers** should care about the enablement defaults and the CMEK/ZDR/HIPAA gap before anyone promises “we’ll do board packs in Claude.”

**Free users** can ignore Docs/Slides for now. The one-Claude merge is scheduled later for Free; Docs/Slides remain paid.

## Short close

The product story here isn’t “Claude invented documents.” It’s that Anthropic finally admitted the chat dump was a bad place to finish work — and that forcing people to choose between chat and Cowork was a UX tax.

If you’re already paying for Pro or Max, try one real artefact this week: a brief that becomes a Doc, then five slides from the same thread, then an export to wherever your colleagues actually open files. Keep the canonical copy outside Claude until version history exists. Ignore the rest of the beta until you’re sure the sharing and compliance model matches how you ship.

Does it shorten the bounce between thinking and something someone else can open? That’s the test that matters.

medium.titulo: Stop Pointing Claude Code at an Empty Folder
medium.resumo: The most underrated variable in agentic coding is not the prompt. It is the repository the agent wakes up in.
medium.conteudo_html:
The most underrated variable in agentic coding is not the prompt. It is the repository the agent wakes up in.

Spend ten minutes in any React Native community right now and you will find developers trading prompts for Claude Code like they are rare cards. Longer prompts. Structured prompts. Prompts with role-play preambles and output contracts.

Almost nobody talks about the other input: the codebase itself. And in my experience running agentic tools on mobile projects, that input matters more.

An empty folder is a hundred invisible decisions

When you point a coding agent at nothing, you are not delegating a feature. You are delegating your entire architecture.

Ask an agent to “build a habit tracker with streaks and reminders” in a blank directory and it must silently decide: which navigation approach, which styling system, how state is managed, where API calls live, how files are organized, how errors are handled, what the theming story is, and dozens of smaller conventions you will live with for the life of the project.

Each individual decision is usually defensible. The problem is the combination. You get an architecture nobody on your team chose, assembled from the statistical average of every public repository the model has seen. It works in the demo. It becomes archaeology the first time a human has to extend it.

Agents are excellent at following conventions and mediocre at inventing them. An empty folder forces them to invent.

React Native makes this worse than most ecosystems, because the ecosystem is genuinely fragmented. Navigation alone has multiple mainstream answers. So does styling. So does state. So does the backend layer. A blank-slate agent picks one path per run, which also means two sessions on two features can drift toward two different philosophies inside the same app.

The fix: give the agent something to imitate

Here is the behavior that changes everything: coding agents pattern-match aggressively against the code that already exists in the repo. Put a well-structured screen in front of Claude Code and ask for a similar one, and it will mirror the file layout, the naming, the styling approach, and the data-fetching pattern almost every time.

That means the highest-leverage thing you can do happens before the first prompt: start from a codebase that already encodes the decisions you want.

This is where starter templates quietly became more valuable in the agent era, not less. A good Expo starter with auth, navigation, theming, and a backend layer already wired is no longer just saved setup time. It is a constraint system. Every convention in it becomes a rail the agent runs on, so the code it generates for feature five looks like the code in feature one.

The practical loop looks like this:

Start from a maintained starter. Pick one whose stack matches what you would have chosen anyway. We curate nineteen React Native and Expo templates over at AppLighter for exactly this reason: a template you would happily extend by hand is the same template an agent will happily extend for you.

Write the conventions down. Claude Code reads a project-level CLAUDE.md file at the start of every session and treats it as standing instructions: architecture notes, coding standards, the commands to run, the patterns to follow. Ten minutes spent describing “screens live here, styling works like this, never touch the auth layer without asking” pays for itself on every subsequent prompt.

Then prompt for features, not foundations. With the substrate in place, your prompts get shorter and better. “Add a paywall screen matching the settings screen’s structure” is a great agent task. “Build me an app” never was.

Where this honestly breaks down

I will not pretend templates solve everything, because two failure modes are real.

Stale starters poison the well. An agent imitates whatever it sees, including outdated patterns. A template that has not kept up with current Expo conventions teaches the agent yesterday’s architecture with total confidence. Maintenance cadence matters more than feature count when you evaluate a starter.

Over-opinionated starters fight the agent. If a template layers heavy custom abstractions over standard APIs, the agent will sometimes bypass them and write vanilla code alongside, and now you have two styles again. The best agent substrates are boringly conventional: standard patterns, clear folders, minimal magic.

The template is not the product. It is the set of decisions you no longer have to defend, session after session.

The takeaway

The prompt-engineering conversation is fun, but it optimizes the last mile. The first mile is the repository. Give Claude Code an empty folder and you get averaged-out architecture; give it a clean, conventional, maintained starting point plus a short conventions file, and the same model produces code that looks like your team wrote it.

Choose the repo before you write the prompt. Everything downstream gets easier.

If you are running Claude Code or any agent on a React Native project, I would love to hear what your starting point was and whether the output drifted. Drop a comment, and a clap helps this reach the next developer about to prompt into a blank directory.

medium.resumo: I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks…
medium.conteudo_html:
I set out to build a proper shortcuts library, not a toy. I hand-wrote the React core, then used Claude Code to take it to six frameworks in record time. Then npm nearly filibustered both of us at the finish line.

Full disclosure, right up top: I wrote the original React hook myself, by hand, no assistance. Everything past that (turning it into a proper package, generalizing it to five more frameworks, writing the test suite, and hunting down the bugs below) was done with Claude Code. I’m not burying that in a footnote. It’s the actual subject of this post.

This didn’t start as a weekend hack that accidentally grew legs. I sat down wanting to build a real shortcuts library, the kind of thing that could declare keyboard, mouse, and wheel shortcuts as plain strings, things like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", "CMD+Z", "DOUBLE_LEFT_BUTTON", and wire them up to handlers without a single hand-rolled addEventListener anywhere in your app. I built the React core myself, from scratch, no assistance. That part was always going to be React-only in my head, at first, a solid foundation before anything else.

But “something big” was the goal from day one, not an afterthought, and a shortcuts library that only works in React isn’t big, it’s a hook with a README. So rather than spend weeks personally relearning the lifecycle quirks of five frameworks I don’t use day to day, I brought in Claude Code and pointed it at the goal directly: take this React implementation and turn it into a real, multi-framework package. Quickly. What came back, and how fast it came back, is the actual subject of this post, including the part where the framework support turned out to be the easy half and the real work was a build tool arguing with itself and npm’s auth system treating us both like we were smuggling a package past customs.

TL;DR

  • The goal from day one was a real, multi-framework shortcuts library, not a side hook.
  • I wrote the React core by hand. Claude Code did the rest of what’s below, fast.
  • It pulled the event-handling logic into one framework-agnostic ShortcutsManager class.
  • Then wrote a thin adapter for each framework as its own subpath export: /react, /vue, /svelte, /solid, /preact, /angular.
  • Its own test suite caught two genuinely funny bugs in its own adapters, and fixed both.
  • Publishing got blocked by 2FA, then by a stale global npm token, then by a token scoped to the wrong account. In that order. On the same package.
  • It’s live: npm install browser-shortcuts.

01 One core, six costumes

The instinct when you want to “support more frameworks” is to go rewrite the library six times. Claude Code’s instinct, thankfully, was to resist that: six slightly-different implementations means six slightly-different bugs, forever. Instead it pulled the entire event-listening brain out of my original hook, the part that listens on window, normalizes a KeyboardEvent into a string like "CTRL+SHIFT+F", and dispatches it to listeners, into a plain class with no framework opinions at all.

class ShortcutsManager {
  on(shortcut, callback) { /* register */ }
  off(shortcut, callback) { /* unregister */ }
  attach(target = window) { /* returns a disposer */ }
}

Every framework adapter is now just this class wearing a costume appropriate to its house party: React kept my original Context Provider and useShortcut hook, rebuilt on top of the shared core. Vue got a plugin and a composable. Svelte got setupShortcuts() plus a hook that reads Svelte's context. Solid got a Provider built on its own context primitive. Angular got an injectable singleton service with DestroyRef-powered cleanup. Preact got, and I want you to sit with how funny this is, the exact same code as React, because Preact's hooks API is basically a very polite tribute act.

react preact vue svelte solid angular

One brain, six faces, and a tsup config with seven separate build entries so nobody importing browser-shortcuts/svelte accidentally drags React into their bundle.

02 The bugs were the fun part

Claude Code wrote a vitest suite that exercises the core and all six adapters: mount, fire the shortcut, unmount, confirm it stopped firing. Thirty-two tests. Along the way that suite turned up two bugs in its own freshly-written code, which it then diagnosed and fixed without me touching a line. Watching an AI catch and root-cause its own bugs is a strange kind of satisfying, like watching someone proofread their own essay out loud and actually catch the typos.

⚠ Bug 01

Solid cleaned up a cleanup function that didn’t exist

This one took the longest to run down, and it’s the kind of bug that makes you question your grip on reality. The Solid provider called onCleanup() to remove its event listeners on unmount. It compiled fine. It ran fine. It just... never actually cleaned up. No error, no warning most of the time, just a listener that outlived the component that created it.

The actual cause: in the test environment, solid-js and solid-js/web were being loaded as two separate module instances, each with its own private copy of Solid's internal "current owner" tracking variable. The component's onCleanup call registered against one copy of that variable; the root's dispose() function tore down the other. Two universes, politely ignoring each other.

Fix: since these components render no real DOM, Claude Code stopped going through solid-js/web's render() in tests entirely and drove everything through solid-js's own createRoot instead: one module, one owner, one universe.

⚠ Bug 02

Angular’s tests demanded a hazing ritual

To test one @Injectable class, it needed: zone.js (Angular's change-detection engine, which apparently just refuses to exist without it), @angular/compiler (for JIT test compilation), @angular/platform-browser-dynamic, a TestBed.initTestEnvironment() call, and a fight with Vite 8's new decorator transform before any of that would even parse. Angular decorators plus a brand-new test bundler is apparently not a combination anyone has smoothed over yet.

Fix: all of the above, added one at a time, in the order the error messages demanded them. Angular testing is basically Dark Souls with dependency injection, and I mean that as a compliment.

If your test suite doesn’t surprise you at least once, you didn’t test hard enough, and it doesn’t matter who, or what, wrote the tests.

03 Publishing: the real boss fight

Writing six framework adapters was, weirdly, the calm part of this project. The final boss was npm publish.

Round one: a flat 403, "Two-factor authentication or granular access token with bypass 2FA enabled is required to publish packages." Fine, I made a token with bypass-2FA explicitly enabled. Still failed.

Round two: turns out the token I’d carefully configured in my project’s .npmrc was being silently ignored, because the package lives inside an npm workspace and npm refuses to read a workspace member's own .npmrc for auth. The token actually being used was a stale one sitting in my global ~/.npmrc, created before I'd ever heard the words "bypass 2FA."

The actual lesson: most auth failures aren’t “is this credential valid,” they’re “which credential is even being sent.” Check that first. It’ll save you a lot of staring at error messages that are technically true but pointing at the wrong culprit.

Round three: fixed the global token, got a brand new error: a 404 on a package name that definitely exists. Turned out the new token had been scoped to the wrong account context during setup. Once that was sorted, the actual publish took about four seconds. The npm CLI does not care how much of an emotional journey you just had.

04 If you’re staring at your own single-framework library

Here’s the encouraging part, because this whole post could read like a cautionary tale and it isn’t one: generalizing a library across frameworks is genuinely more approachable than it looks from the outside, and it’s a legitimately good use of an AI pair. The pattern (one core, thin adapters) is well-established, the failure modes are well-documented across enough GitHub issues to be learnable, and the tests catch you the moment you drift. You don’t need a grand unifying abstraction. You need one honest class that does the actual work, and the discipline to keep every framework’s adapter dumb, just lifecycle glue, nothing clever. The moment an adapter starts containing real logic, you’ve built six libraries again, not one.

And write the tests, whoever’s writing the code. Not because tests are virtuous, but because they’re the fastest way to find out where the mental model of “how this framework works” is quietly wrong. Both bugs above were a gap between what was assumed and what was actually true, and they only surfaced because a test insisted on checking.

I’ll say the quiet part plainly, since it’s the actual point of this post: I wrote the React hook, Claude Code wrote the rest of what’s above, and I’m comfortable putting my name on both halves. It’s live now, MIT-licensed, zero runtime dependencies of its own:

npm install browser-shortcuts
  • browser-shortcuts/react and /preact: a Provider and a useShortcut hook
  • browser-shortcuts/vue: a plugin and a composable
  • browser-shortcuts/svelte: setupShortcuts() plus a hook
  • browser-shortcuts/solid: a context Provider
  • browser-shortcuts/angular: an injectable service

If you use one of these frameworks and shortcuts in your app currently involve a stray addEventListener in a useEffect somewhere, I'd love for you to try it and tell me what breaks. That's genuinely the fastest way to find bug number three.

Side note

This isn’t the first thing I’ve shipped to npm, and it won’t be the last. If you’re curious what else is out there:

  • antoniookoro.com, my portfolio, with writing, projects, and how to reach me
  • vue3-form, form validation for Vue 3 and the composition API
  • bootstrap-vue-datatable, a datatable plugin for Vue and Bootstrap
  • storagedotjs, a small, lightweight API over Local Storage

Written by Antonio Okoro, built with Claude Code.
Thoughts, bug reports, and “well actually”s about Solid’s owner tracking are all welcome.

corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Terça-feira | 22 de setembro de 2026

Hoje é o dia do lançamento oficial do Adidas Adios Pro 5, um dos tênis mais esperados do ano. Após meses de vazamentos e especulações, a principal novidade confirmada é a mudança na estrutura da placa de carbono. Os tradicionais Energyrods foram substituídos por um novo sistema que contorna toda a borda do tênis. Além disso, o modelo aparenta estar mais leve. Embora o lançamento global seja hoje, alguns influenciadores já “furaram o bloqueio” e postaram sobre o tênis, como foi o caso do Kayo Borghi, que mostrou o modelo em primeira mão. A expectativa é que muitos atletas patrocinados utilizem o Adios Pro 5 na Maratona de Berlim no próximo domingo.

Maratona de Boston: começa o drama do tempo de corte

A organização da Maratona de Boston divulgou que recebeu 33.656 inscrições de corredores que atingiram o tempo de qualificação. Como o número de vagas para qualificados é de aproximadamente 24 mil, agora começa o período de tensão para saber qual será a nota de corte. Em grupos de corredores, a especulação é que o tempo necessário seja entre 4 minutos e 30 segundos a 5 minutos abaixo do índice oficial. Uma novidade para esta edição é que a organização irá sortear mil vagas entre os corredores que atingiram o índice, mas não foram selecionados pela nota de corte. As outras formas de participação continuam sendo através de agências de turismo, patrocinadores e programas de caridade.

Recorde quebrado na Meia Maratona do Sol em Natal

A Meia Maratona do Sol, realizada no último domingo em Natal, foi marcada pela quebra do recorde do percurso no masculino. A prova, que tem largada e chegada na Arena das Dunas, é a única do Nordeste com selo da World Athletics. O grande campeão foi José Márcio Leão da Silva, que completou os 21 km em 1:06:22, estabelecendo a nova marca a ser batida. No total, 5.979 pessoas concluíram os 5 km, 5.304 os 10 km e 5.487 a meia maratona.

Inscrições para a Muralha Marathon têm data marcada

A Muralha Up and Down Marathon, uma prova exclusivamente de maratona que alterna seu percurso entre subida (“Up”) e descida (“Down”) a cada ano, já tem data para a abertura das inscrições. A próxima edição será no dia 15 de agosto de 2027, com o trajeto “Down”, partindo de Visconde de Mauá e chegando em Penedo. As inscrições, em lote único, abrirão no dia 6 de outubro de 2026, às 19:42:19, e costumam esgotar em poucas horas.

Corrida do Iron Maiden confirmada em Curitiba

Após a grande procura pela edição de São Paulo, que acontece no dia 10 de dezembro, a corrida temática do Iron Maiden, “Iron Ron Maiden”, foi confirmada em Curitiba. A prova na capital paranaense ocorrerá no dia 13 de dezembro. A cidade tem uma forte ligação com a banda, que inclusive possui uma cerveja fabricada localmente. As inscrições para a etapa de Curitiba devem abrir em breve.
